<explanation>
Below is a tailored guide for drawing a system‐design diagram of QueryWeaver. We’ll break the app into its major pieces, show how they interact, highlight the patterns in use, and give you tips on how to render it clearly.

1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - QueryWeaver is a full-stack web application.  
   - Backend: FastAPI (Python) providing REST and MCP HTTP endpoints.  
   - Frontend: TypeScript + Jinja2 templates (served by the backend).  
   - Core functionality: convert user natural-language questions into SQL (Text2SQL) via graph-powered schema understanding and LLM calls.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top level:  
     • api/ – FastAPI backend modules  
     • app/ – TypeScript frontend (static assets + Jinja2 templates)  
     • tests/ – unit and E2E tests (Playwright)  
     • Dockerfile, Makefile, Pipfile, workflows – CI/CD and deployment configuration  
   - api/ subfolders:  
     • routes/ – HTTP routes (auth, graphs, tokens, database)  
     • agents/ – “chain‐of‐agents” that perform analysis, relevancy filtering, follow-ups, formatting  
     • loaders/ – graph schema loaders (generic JSON, MySQL, PostgreSQL)  
     • memory/ – in-process memory/tooling (graphiti_tool)  
     • auth/ – OAuth handlers (Google, GitHub), user management  
     • app_factory.py, extensions.py – application factory and FastAPI extension registration  
     • config.py – environment and LLM configuration (Azure/OpenAI)  
   - app/ structure:  
     • public/ – compiled CSS, images, icons, fonts  
     • templates/ – Jinja2 templates for pages/components  
     • ts/ – TypeScript modules for UI logic (chat, graphs, modals, etc.)

3. Examine README for insights  
   - Describes REST endpoints (/graphs, /graphs/{id}/data, POST /graphs, POST /graphs/{id})  
   - Mentions optional MCP server surface or client usage  
   - OAuth flows, streaming via SSE (`|||FALKORDB_MESSAGE_BOUNDARY|||`)  
   - Tech stack: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Python 3.12+, Node.js, npm, Playwright, Docker, MCP protocol

4. Main components to depict  
   a. Client (Browser) – UI rendered via Jinja2 + TypeScript, communicates over HTTPS  
   b. API Server – FastAPI/Uvicorn application  
   c. Authentication subsystem – OAuth providers (Google, GitHub), session cookies, API tokens  
   d. Agent pipeline – analysis_agent, relevancy_agent, follow_up_agent, response_formatter_agent  
   e. Loaders & Graph Store – MySQL/PostgreSQL loaders, graph_loader, base_loader, memory/graphiti_tool  
   f. LLM Service – Azure OpenAI or OpenAI endpoints  
   g. FalkorDB (optional) – external MCP server or internal graph database  
   h. Persistence layer – user/account DB (if any), token store  
   i. Tests & CI – shown separately (unit tests, E2E tests, GitHub Actions)

5. Relationships and data flows  
   - Browser → API Server:  
     • GET / (serves HTML/JS/CSS)  
     • AJAX/Fetch/WebSocket for chat sessions (streaming SSE)  
   - API Server ↔ OAuth Providers:  
     • Redirect flow for Google/GitHub OAuth → session cookie  
   - API Server → Agents pipeline → LLM Service:  
     • Streaming requests/responses for Text2SQL chain  
   - API Server → Loaders → Schema store:  
     • On graph upload or database introspection  
   - API Server → FalkorDB (MCP):  
     • If acting as MCP client or hosting MCP endpoints  
   - API Server ↔ Persistence:  
     • User, token, graph metadata storage (could be a relational store)  
   - Tests → API Server & Browser:  
     • Unit tests call modules directly  
     • E2E tests use Playwright to exercise UI and API

6. Architectural patterns & design principles  
   - MVC‐style separation: templates (view), API routes (controller), agents/loaders (model)  
   - “Chain of Responsibility” for agent pipeline  
   - Plugin pattern: loaders and memory modules swappable via base classes  
   - Streaming responses (SSE) for real‐time chat  
   - Optional microservice (MCP) interface for reuse in other contexts  

7. Diagram‐drawing guidelines  
   - Use boxes for each major component (Frontend, Backend, Agents, Loaders, External Services)  
   - Group related submodules inside each component box (e.g., inside Backend: routes, auth, agents, loaders)  
   - Draw directional arrows for request/response flows:  
     • Solid arrows for main data flows (browser→API, API→LLM, API→DB)  
     • Dashed arrows for optional/conditional flows (MCP server, external graph DB)  
   - Color‐code by component type:  
     • Frontend (blue), Backend (green), External services (orange), Data stores (purple)  
   - Label each arrow with the protocol or endpoint (HTTPS, SSE, OAuth, MCP HTTP)  
   - Use different shapes/icons for third-party services (e.g., cloud icon for Azure/OpenAI, cylinder for DB)  
   - Include a legend for colors and shapes to keep it clear  

8. Tailoring for this full‐stack application  
   - Emphasize separation of concerns:  
     • UI rendering vs. API logic vs. agent chain vs. persistence  
   - Highlight streaming SSE flow between backend and frontend (boundary marker)  
   - Show OAuth redirect flows and token usage paths  
   - Call out the loader plugins and graph memory as key extensibility points  
   - Depict the choice between embedded MCP server vs. external MCP client  

By following these steps and including all the labeled boxes, arrows, colors, and shapes noted above, you will produce an accurate, detailed system‐design diagram that captures the essential architecture of QueryWeaver without overthinking it. Aim for clarity: group subcomponents, show all interactions, and call out the critical LLM and graph‐loading pathways.
</explanation>
